issues.legal_issue: A criminal conviction cannot be sustained when the evidence leaves reasonable doubt about the identification of the assailants and attribution of the fatal injuries.
material_facts: The shooting occurred at night in an agricultural field, and the scene evidence and witnesses did not establish that sufficient light was available for identification.
Witness accounts conflicted about who fired the shots.
The medical evidence did not identify whether the fatal wounds were caused by a rifle or a gun, and weapons attributed to two different accused had been recovered.
The witnesses to the weapon-recovery panchnama did not support the prosecution, and the recovery lacked corroboration from an independent source.
The evidence included injured eyewitnesses, but the identification and attribution evidence remained uncertain.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The convictions under Sections 302 and 307 read with Section 34 of the IPC and Section 25(c) of the Arms Act were set aside, and the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Proof of motive is relevant but is a double-edged consideration and merely adds to the value of eyewitness evidence. In the circumstances of competing firearms and hostile recovery witnesses, prudence required corroboration from another source for the weapon recovery. The Court applied these principles in reviewing the convictions under Sections 302 and 307 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 25(c) of the Arms Act.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and occurrence_in_darkness_without_evidence_of_sufficient_light and eyewitness_accounts_conflict_about_shooter and fatal_weapon_attribution_is_uncertain and weapon_recovery_lacks_independent_corroboration

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused challenged a criminal conviction on appeal.
predicates.occurrence_in_darkness_without_evidence_: The prosecution evidence placed the occurrence at night, but did not establish sufficient light for witnesses to identify the assailants.
predicates.eyewitness_accounts_conflict_about_shoot: The eyewitness accounts differed about who fired the shots.
predicates.fatal_weapon_attribution_is_uncertain: The medical evidence did not establish which of the firearms caused the fatal wounds.
predicates.weapon_recovery_lacks_independent_corrob: The independent witnesses to the weapon recovery did not support it, and the recovery had no corroboration from another source.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction is challenged and the identification, account of the shooter, fatal-weapon attribution, and recovery evidence are uncertain in the stated ways, the conviction is set aside on reasonable doubt.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with concurrent factual findings in an appeal when those findings are perverse or result from erroneous appreciation of the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court had both convicted the appellant.
The High Court had not properly appreciated the oral evidence, other evidence, and the appellant’s challenges to the prosecution case.
The Supreme Court found the lower courts’ findings perverse and their appreciation of the evidence improper.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court interfered with the concurrent findings and set aside the conviction.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court ordinarily does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact unless they are shown to be perverse. It may review the evidence where its appreciation is erroneous. The Court relied on Mahesh Dattatray Thirthkar v. State of Maharashtra, (2009) 11 SCC 141.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court_from_concurrent_: A party brought an appeal to the Supreme Court challenging factual findings reached by both lower courts.
predicates.findings_are_perverse_or_based_on_errone: The Supreme Court found that the concurrent findings were perverse or resulted from erroneous appreciation of the evidence.

issues.definition: When the Supreme Court hears an appeal from concurrent factual findings and finds them perverse or based on erroneous appreciation of evidence, it may set them aside.
